title: Designing Work That Motivates
text:
In the 1970s the organizational psychologists Richard Hackman and Greg Oldham asked what makes a job itself motivating. They proposed that five features matter most: skill variety (using different skills), task identity (doing a whole, visible piece of work from start to finish), task significance (affecting other people), autonomy (freedom in how to do it) and feedback (knowing how well it is going).

According to their theory, these features create three key psychological states. People feel their work is meaningful, they feel responsible for the outcomes, and they know the results of their efforts. Those states, in turn, lead to stronger motivation, higher satisfaction and better work.

To test the idea, they surveyed several hundred employees working in dozens of different jobs in seven organizations, and also gathered ratings from supervisors and observers. Jobs that scored higher on the five features were linked to more internal motivation and satisfaction, and to some extent to better performance and less absence. The effects were strongest for people who wanted to grow in their work. The model became one of the most widely used tools for redesigning jobs.
lesson: Motivation is often built into the job, not added by speeches. Give people whole tasks, freedom in how to do them, a view of who benefits, and clear feedback.
source: Hackman, J. R., and Oldham, G. R. (1976). Motivation through the design of work: Test of a theory. Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 16(2), 250-279.
